title: Committing, Renaming & Resource Limits 🧪
description: Save container state as a new image, rename containers, and control CPU/memory.

slides.title: Saving Container State: `docker commit` 💾
slides.content:
# Turn a Container into an Image

If you’ve modified a container (installed packages, changed files) and want to reuse that state, you can **commit** it as a new image.

```bash
docker commit [OPTIONS] CONTAINER [REPOSITORY[:TAG]]
```

**Example:**
```bash
docker commit my-debug-container my-debug-image:latest
```

This creates a new image with all the changes made to the container.

> ⚠️ Committing is **not** the recommended way to build images; Dockerfiles are much better (reproducible, versioned). But `commit` is useful for quick snapshots and debugging.

quizData.question: Why is using `docker commit` often discouraged for production images?

options.text: It always produces larger images than Dockerfiles.
It doesn’t record the commands used to build the image, making it less reproducible.
It cannot push images to registries.
It only works on Linux containers.

quizData.explanation: `docker commit` creates an image from a container’s state, but there’s no Dockerfile – you can’t see what changes were made. Dockerfiles are transparent and repeatable.

slides.title: Commit Demo 🧪
slides.content: Make a change inside a container and save it:
slides.codeSnippet:
# Run a container
docker run -d --name devbox alpine sleep 3600

# Install a package inside (e.g., curl)
docker exec devbox apk add curl

# Verify curl is installed
docker exec devbox curl --version

# Commit the container as a new image
docker commit devbox my-alpine-curl:1.0

# Now run a container from the new image
docker run --rm my-alpine-curl:1.0 curl --version

# Cleanup
docker stop devbox
docker rm devbox

slides.title: Renaming Containers 🏷️
slides.content:
# `docker rename`

If you gave a container a poor name, you can rename it:

```bash
docker rename OLD_NAME NEW_NAME
```

**Example:**
```bash
docker rename hopeful_swirles frontend
```

The container ID remains the same. Works on both running and stopped containers.

quizData.question: Renaming a container changes its unique container ID.
quizData.explanation: The ID is immutable. Only the name label is changed.

slides.title: Setting Resource Limits 🎛️
slides.content:
# Control CPU and Memory

Containers share the host kernel; without limits, one container can hog all resources. Set limits at runtime:

```bash
docker run -d --name limited --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 nginx
```

- `--memory` (or `-m`): maximum memory (e.g., `512m` for 512 MB, `2g` for 2 GB).
- `--cpus`: how many CPU cores the container can use (e.g., `1.5` = one and a half cores).

You can also set `--memory-swap` (swap space) and `--cpu-shares` (relative weight).

slides.title: Resource Limits in Action 🔒
slides.content: Limit memory and CPU for a container:
slides.codeSnippet:
# Run a container with a 256 MB memory limit and 0.5 CPU
docker run -d --name constrained --memory=256m --cpus=0.5 alpine sleep 600

# Inspect the limits
docker inspect -f 'Memory: {{.HostConfig.Memory}} CPUs: {{.HostConfig.NanoCpus}}' constrained

quizData.question: Which `docker run` flag sets a memory limit of 1 GB?
quizData.explanation: `-m` or `--memory` sets the hard memory limit. The unit can be `m` for megabytes or `g` for gigabytes.

slides.title: Restart Policies 🔄
slides.content:
# Keep Containers Alive

Control what happens when a container exits:

- `--restart no` (default) – don’t restart.
- `--restart on-failure[:max-retries]` – restart only if exit code is non‑zero.
- `--restart always` – always restart, even on daemon restart.
- `--restart unless-stopped` – always restart, unless you explicitly stop it.

**Example:**
```bash
docker run -d --restart=always nginx
```

Useful for production services to survive crashes.

quizData.question: If you want a container to restart automatically unless you explicitly run `docker stop`, which restart policy should you use?
quizData.explanation: `unless-stopped` restarts the container even after daemon restart, but not if you intentionally stopped it with `docker stop`.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: ## Use `--restart=always` for development, but consider orchestration (like Docker Swarm or Kubernetes) for production‑grade restart logic.
